newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-RONALDO MOVE ON HOLD WHILE FIFA CONSIDER EVIDENCE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-RONALDO MOVE ON HOLD WHILE FIFA CONSIDER EVIDENCE.

text.p: FIFA, world soccer's governing body, said on Monday that any decision on the legality of Ronaldo's transfer from Barcelona to Internazionale Milan might not be made until the end of this month.

That effectively means the move is on hold while FIFA study documents from both clubs -- and also consider their response to the European Union whose intervention in the transfer has further complicated an already labyrinthine situation.

"Documents from both clubs are here and we have statements from the two sides" said FIFA spokesman Andreas Herren, adding that no date for a meeting by the Players Status Committee had been set. "We would like to deal with this quickly, hopefully by the end of the month."
By then however, FIFA's decision could be irrelevant, following a statement issued by the European Commission on Friday that appears to clear the way for Ronaldo's move to Italy.

The tug-of-war between Barcelona and Internazionale over who owns the world football player of the year has been further complicated by the European Commission's warning to FIFA, that its transfer regulations contravened European Union laws.
The Commission's statement said, that a recent circular by FIFA "constitutes an unjustified obstacle to the free movement of workers".

That is a right granted to footballers by the European Court of Justice in the landmark Bosman ruling of December 1995, which outlawed transfer fees for out of contract players within the EU and banned nationality restrictions in domestic and international club competitions.
While Ronaldo is under contract to Barcelona until 2004, a withdrawal clause in his Spanish contract has allowed him to "buyout" his deal for a reported $27.5 million.

But the Spanish Football Federation has refused to issue a transfer certificate for the 20-year-old Brazilian on the grounds that such "buyouts" or withdrawal clauses are valid for domestic transfers only.
That appears to be a position supported by FIFA rules which state, that a player cannot buy out his contract for the purposes of obtaining an international transfer.
Herren, acknowledged that FIFA had received a copy of the European Commission statement on Friday and, "would respond with a letter.
"But it is a lot to digest and we will not be responding through the media," he added.

The European Commission statement, signed by Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert and Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn said FIFA's circular appeared to maintain a system which had already been ruled illegal by the European Court of Justice and appeared also to contravene EU regulations.
It said they hoped FIFA would "take this preliminary position into account", a signal that the Commission might take the matter further should they not be happy with the outcome.
